A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WIND research work. All 30 pages of each version, including appendices A–C, provide readable text, equations, tables and figures sufficient for comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting, downscaling, sparse-reconstruction, conservation and Storm Bernd experiments, with quantitative and graphical results throughout the paper and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and additionally reports forecasting comparisons for 2020 and measured inference runtime and memory usage.

M1.justification: The UViT architecture, diffusion-forcing objective, omission of noise-level conditioning, DDIM sampling and MMPS task operators remain unchanged. The new inference algorithms document the existing procedure rather than establish a changed method.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same ERA5 atmospheric variables and forecasting, downscaling, reconstruction, conservation and warmer-climate tasks. WeatherBench2 already supplies the data in v1; the additional 2020 forecasting comparison changes evaluation sampling, not the represented task or domain.

E2.justification: Table B.2 adds reported comparisons against IFS ENS, GenCast, operational GenCast, ArchesWeatherGen and probabilistic climatology. This substantially extends forecasting comparisons beyond the retained AR-UViT surrogates. The downscaling and reconstruction comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds a separate 2020 forecast evaluation at 24, 120 and 240 hours, plus runtime and memory benchmarking with 15/30 DDIM steps and 1–3 CG iterations. Existing accuracy-evaluation settings remain unchanged, including the unresolved discrepancy between 24 initial conditions in the text and 100 in the forecast caption.

E4.justification: Appendix B.6 newly analyzes computational cost as DDIM steps and CG iterations vary, quantifying the overhead of guidance. The long-rollout, spectral, diurnal-harmonic and Storm Bernd guidance analyses are retained; their relocation does not introduce new analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix B.6 newly specifies that timing measurements average 10 runs after three burn-in runs. This concerns the added runtime experiment; existing forecast and Storm Bernd ensemble sizes are unchanged, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: Table B.2 adds substantial forecasting results: for example, 120-hour T2m CRPS is 0.624 for WIND and 0.482 for GenCast. Table B.1 adds runtime and memory results, including 0.5573 seconds unguided versus 4.5189 seconds with two CG iterations at 15 DDIM steps. These are additional evaluations; the original three RMSE tables and reported Storm Bernd outcomes remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3 and new Appendix B.4 explicitly derive the existing MMPS approximation using predictive covariance, operator linearization, the assumption of negligible covariance derivatives, and a CG linear system. v1 largely delegates these steps to the cited method. Existing diffusion, training-loss, DDIM and conservation equations are retained.

C1.justification: The central claim of one pretrained model solving multiple tasks without fine-tuning remains. However, the abstract narrows physically consistent counterfactual storylines to exploration under prescribed thermodynamic perturbations, and general conservation claims become specifically global dry air mass conservation.

C2.justification: v2 substantially qualifies the scientific interpretation: Storm Bernd becomes a single-event proof of concept rather than evidence for strict causal predictions, uniform warming perturbations are acknowledged as simplified, and local conservation is explicitly unenforced. It also interprets late-lead calibration through climatological saturation and explains the complementary roles of diffusion forcing and MMPS.

D1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 and Appendix B.5 substantially expand implementation documentation for MMPS, Jacobian products and both inference modes. Appendix B.6 adds benchmark hardware and resource requirements. Existing architecture and training hyperparameters remain stable, while v1's explicit code-repository link is removed; actual repository availability cannot be determined from the PDFs.

R1.justification: v2 adds relevant references including Efron on covariance estimation, Rackow on climate robustness, Subich on scoring effects, and Qian and Yang on reconstruction and assimilation. It removes the extended attribution background and several associated citations. The broader positioning as a unified atmospheric foundation model remains.

P1.justification: The approach and discussion receive substantial rewrites, with a dedicated task-operator subsection and expanded inference exposition. The counterfactual narrative is recast around warmer-climate evaluation, temporal-downscaling discussion moves to the appendix, and the attribution background is removed. Conflict-of-interest and impact statements are also added.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout, redraws the overview, adds a guidance schematic, two tables and three algorithm displays, and reformats sparse-reconstruction maps. Existing figures are extensively relocated, including the main-text reconstruction example and appendix spectral plots; these moves preserve their underlying evidence.

improvement.justification: v2 improves assessment of WIND through external forecasting comparisons, measured guidance costs and clearer boundaries on climate and conservation claims. The expanded inference documentation also helps reproducibility. These gains are tempered by removal of the code-access link and the unresolved forecast-initialization discrepancy, supporting a limited overall improvement.
